sections.heading: Dialogue I, Knot ii, part 1 (printed pp. 9–17)
rows: [p. 9] [Margin: Nodus II. Mundum non esse infinitum.] Ereu. Quoniam utrique sedit eadem voluntas, ego quomodo renitar? hoc itaque primum ex te sciscitari velim, Andabata, an ex demonstratione tua consequi putes stellas numero infinitas esse, coelique spatia non parvitate nostra, sed sua ipsorum mole ultra omnem cogitationem esse diffusa? Cum enim finiti ad infinitum non sit comparatio, vides quo excessu divina amplietur gloria, si infinita reapse sint quae in hominum usum caelestis effundit benignitas.

[p. 9] [Margin: Knot II. That the world is not infinite.] Ereu. Since in both [of you] the same will has settled [sedit], how should I resist [renitar]? This therefore I would wish first to inquire [sciscitari] from you, Andabata: whether you think it follows from your demonstration that the stars are infinite in number, and that the spaces of the heaven are spread out beyond all thought, not by our smallness [parvitate], but by their own mass [mole]? For since there is no comparison of the finite to the infinite, you see by what excess the divine glory is amplified, if the things which the heavenly benignity pours out for the use of men are infinite in reality [reapse].

Andab. Recte colligis, neque ego aegre feram deductum esse ex dictis meis tale corollarium. Legi enim quae summi Philosophi copiosissime de infinito scripserunt, neque quic-[p. 10]quam video contra infinitatem afferri, quod probabili solutione non diluatur.

Andab. You gather [colligis] rightly, nor shall I bear [it] ill that such a corollary has been deduced from my sayings. For I have read the things which the highest Philosophers have written most copiously about the infinite, nor do I see any-[p. 10]thing brought forward against infinity [infinitatem] which is not washed away [diluatur] by a probable [probabili] solution.

Ereu. Neque ego tibi obiectis multis fastidium ciebo. Unum est quod expediri mihi desidero, idque ipsum non dubito, quin millies tibi auditum cogitatumque sit, ut haerendum non sit quid respondeas. Putasne ex infinitis stellis aliquam unam ab his aedibus per infinita milliaria, vel si mavis, passus vel digitos absistere? Et ne forte de stella tibi ambiguitas oriatur, de parte quacumque coelestium illorum spatiorum respondeto, ullusne palmus infinite sit remotus?

Ereu. Nor shall I stir up [ciebo] disgust for you with many objections [obiectis]. There is one [thing] which I desire to be cleared up [expediri] for me, and that very thing, I do not doubt, has been heard and thought by you a thousand times, so that there is no need to hesitate [haerendum non sit] over what you should answer. Do you think that out of the infinite stars some one stands off [absistere] from these houses [aedibus] by infinite miles, or, if you prefer, paces or fingers [digitos]? And lest perhaps an ambiguity should arise for you about [the word] star, answer [respondeto] about any part whatever of those heavenly spaces: is any palm [palmus] infinitely removed?

Andab. Etsi perspectum satis habeam quo tendas, inutiles tamen moras nequaquam nectam, sed quod res est, palam profiteor aliquam coeli partem (siquidem infinitum sit coelum) a nobis ex necessitate, infinito spatio dissidere. Cum enim distantia realis et corporea sit infinita, ex infinitis prorsus partibus, aequalibus pedibus, inquam, et passibus conflatur, qui cum infiniti sint, et alius alium semper excludens, palam est infinitos esse non posse quin aliquis ab infinitis sit exclusus. Vide igitur quid inde inferas.

Andab. Although I hold [it] sufficiently perceived [perspectum] whither you are tending, yet I shall by no means weave [nectam] useless delays, but, as the matter is, I openly profess that some part of the heaven (if indeed the heaven be infinite) of necessity stands apart [dissidere] from us by an infinite space. For since a real and corporeal distance is infinite, it is put together [conflatur] out of altogether infinite parts, out of equal feet, I say, and paces; which, since they are infinite, and one always excluding another, it is plain that they cannot be infinite but that [quin] some one is excluded by infinite [ones]. See therefore what you infer thence.
Ereu. At unicum fortassis in eadem recta linea passum a nobis infinite distare arbitraris, an vero concedis plures in eadem linea infinita passus infinite abesse?

Ereu. But do you judge perhaps that a single pace in the same straight line is infinitely distant from us, or do you indeed grant that more [plures] paces in the same infinite line are infinitely away [abesse]?

[p. 11] Andab. Non plures tantummodo sed infinitos, et vide qua evidentia? Esto enim passus unicus qui infinite a nobis sit remotus, contiguus ergo passus iam numeratis abest passibus, quare unicus passus numeratis additus, infinitos effecturus est: quod a veritate alienum esse vel luscus videt. Et quomodo de uno passu institui rationem, sic de qualibet finita multitudine proclive est argumentari, cum finitam multitudinem finitae appositam, infinitam creare non sint admissuri Arithmetici; totum enim hoc ad partes certam mensuram habet, infiniti vero ad finitum nulla est proportio.

[p. 11] Andab. Not more [plures] only, but infinite; and see with what evidence? For let there be [esto] a single pace which is infinitely removed from us; the contiguous pace, therefore, is away [abest] by paces already numbered [numeratis]; wherefore a single pace added to the numbered [paces] is going to make [effecturus est] infinite [paces]: which even a one-eyed man [luscus] sees to be alien from the truth. And in the way that I have set up the reasoning [institui rationem] about one pace, so it is easy [proclive] to argue about any finite multitude whatever, since the Arithmeticians are not going to admit that a finite multitude placed beside [appositam] a finite [one] creates an infinite [one]; for this whole has a certain measure to [its] parts, but of the infinite to the finite there is no proportion.

Ereu. Egregium et quale a te expectare debui, Andabata, responsum tuli. Sed habes virum timidum et non satis sibi fidentem; ne graveris itaque et hoc respondere. Hi passus quos infinitos et infinite distare asseris, suntne eiusdem naturae cum iis quos hic prope nos videmus et tractamus, an aliam aliquam quantitatem nobis narras, cuius dispositio nos lateat, neque satis cum hac nostrate conveniat, ut illi arguendo attribuere fas sit quae nostrae huic inesse comperimus?

Ereu. An excellent [answer], and such as I ought to have expected [expectare debui] from you, Andabata, have I carried off [tuli] as answer. But you have [in me] a man timid and not trusting himself enough; do not therefore be loath [ne graveris] to answer this also. These paces which you assert [to be] infinite and to be infinitely distant, are they of the same nature with those which here near us we see and handle, or are you telling us of some other quantity, whose disposition [dispositio] is hidden from us, nor agrees sufficiently with this home-grown [nostrate] [quantity], so that it be right [fas], in arguing, to attribute to that [quantity] the things which we find to be in this one of ours?

Andab. Parce metu, Ereuni, manet immota quantitatis ratio ut hic, sic illic divisibilis, quales hic partes habet, tales et illic, nulla alia conditione diversas, nisi quod omnem nume-[p. 12]rum limitemque excedant.

Andab. Spare [your] fear [Parce metu], Ereunius: the reason [ratio] of quantity remains unmoved [immota]: as here, so there, divisible; such parts as it has here, such also there, different by no other condition, except that they exceed all num-[p. 12]ber and limit.
Ereu. Agedum itaque unum aliquem passum seligamus, de quo procedat disputatio: quemlibet designato.
Ereu. Come then, let us select some one pace, about which the disputation may proceed: designate [designato] any [one] you like.
Andab. Non facio, neque posse fieri autumo.
Andab. I do not do [it], nor do I reckon [autumo] that it can be done.

Ereu. Satin tibi praesens es qui ex tot millibus et longitudine infinita, neque unum passum esse existimes designabilem, cum ultimo prorsus spiritu eandem illius quantitatis dispositionem edixeris quae sit nostra, nostrae autem hoc vel imprimis competat ut partes signabiles habeat et secabiles.

Ereu. Are you sufficiently present to yourself [Satin tibi praesens es], [you] who think that, out of so many thousands and an infinite length, not even one pace is designable [designabilem], when with quite your last breath [ultimo prorsus spiritu] you declared [edixeris] the disposition of that quantity [to be] the same which is ours, and to ours, moreover, this belongs [competat] even first of all [vel imprimis], that it has parts signable [signabiles] and cuttable [secabiles]?

Andab. Imo tu satin sanus es qui me per infinita illa spatia peregrinatum putes vel peregrinari imperes, ut unum aliquem ex iis passum tibi exhibeam, quos nunquam his oculis aspexi, vel me conspicaturum sperem?

Andab. Nay, are you sufficiently sane [satin sanus es], [you] who think that I have travelled abroad [peregrinatum] through those infinite spaces, or command [me] to travel, so that I may exhibit to you some one pace out of those which I never beheld with these eyes, or hope that I shall catch sight of [them]?

Asphal. Ne saevi Andabata. Mathematico tecum more vel sermone magis agit Ereunius, tu pro Physica consuetudine accipis. Cum designari iubet aliquem passum non hoc agit ut scalpro circumcidas, vel positis animo metis agnoscas? sed ut thesim tuam ad hypothesim revoces, et quos dixisti multos et infinitos esse, de horum uno quolibet, postquam tot sunt, illi agere liceat. Ignorare enim illud non potes, quod pluribus indifferenter seu universaliter competit hoc ipsum singulis singu-[p. 13]lariter competere:

Asphal. Do not rage, Andabata. Ereunius deals with you rather in the Mathematical manner or speech [sermone]; you take [it] according to Physical custom. When he bids some pace to be designated, he does not aim at this [non hoc agit], that you should cut [it] round with a chisel [scalpro], or recognise [it] with boundary-posts [metis] set in [your] mind? but that you should bring back your thesis [thesim] to a hypothesis [hypothesim], and that, of those which you said to be many and infinite, about any one of these, since [postquam] they are so many, it may be allowed to him to treat. For you cannot be ignorant of that: [that] what belongs [competit] to more [things] indifferently or universally, this very thing belongs to each singly [singulis singu-[p. 13]lariter]:

Quare si de infinitis passibus ipsemet pronunciasti, singulos eorum ab hoc conclavi infinite abesse, potestne integrum tibi esse negare hoc ipsum de quoquam singulari esse verum? omni profecto evidentia perspectum est, vel eos passus non esse tales quales hi nostri sunt, reales dico et in natura rerum existentes, terminisque suis pro natura quanti conclusos, Entisque et unius naturam participantes; vel de singulis eorum singulatim verum esse, quod universaliter vere de illis pronunciatum est.

Wherefore if about the infinite paces you yourself have pronounced that each [singulos] of them is infinitely away from this chamber [conclavi], can it be open [integrum] to you to deny that this very thing is true about any singular? Assuredly it is perceived with all evidence: either that those paces are not such as these of ours are—real, I say, and existing in the nature of things, and closed by their own terms [terminis] according to the nature of a quantum [quanti], and participating in the nature of Being [Entis] and of One [unius]—or that about each of them singly [singulatim] that is true which universally has been truly pronounced about them.

Andab. Ast ego tibi Asphali confidenter affirmo, non sic se rem habere, sed quod universim affirmatum est, posse in singularibus fallere. Et tu si magnos illos Authores legisses quibus ego a teneris insuevi, nequaquam ipse dubitares; et ne in posterum eodem luto haereas, evidentissimo exemplo tibi viam expedio.

Andab. But I confidently affirm to you, Asphalius, that the matter does not hold itself so, but that what has been affirmed universally [universim] can fail [fallere] in singulars. And you, if you had read those great Authors to whom I from tender [years] [a teneris] accustomed myself, would by no means yourself doubt; and lest hereafter you stick in the same mud [eodem luto haereas], I clear the way [viam expedio] for you with a most evident example.

Cras eundum mihi est quo hodie debueram, neque sine equo proficisci possum. Est itaque mihi necessarius equus, inferes ergo tu eum mihi necessarium esse quem hodie insedi? pellucet fallacia, nam vel tuo vel Ereunii huius, vel alio conductitio pervehi possim. Ecce quomodo et dum in communi quaeritur, equum esse necessarium ipsa veritas attestatur: et cum ad singularia descensum est, quod communiter affirmabatur, deficit, et non eo usque [p. 14] pertingit ut unum quodlibet determinate afficiat, sic itaque et circa infinitum agitur: dum in communi haeret sermo, de infinitis verum est infinite a nobis dissidere. Si ad singularia descendendum est, nullum invenitur de quo speciatim asseri potest.

Tomorrow I must go whither I ought [debueram] [to have gone] today, nor can I set out without a horse. A horse therefore is necessary to me; will you then infer that that [horse] is necessary to me which I sat on [insedi] today? The fallacy shines through, for I could be carried through either by yours, or by [that] of Ereunius here, or by another hired [one]. See how, both while it is asked in common [in communi], the truth itself attests that a horse is necessary, and, when the descent has been made to singulars, what was affirmed commonly fails, and does not reach [p. 14] so far [eo usque] that it affects any one whatever determinately [determinate]. So therefore it goes [agitur] also concerning the infinite: while the discourse [sermo] sticks in common, it is true of infinite [things] that they stand apart [dissidere] infinitely from us. If one must descend to singulars, none is found of which [it] can be asserted specifically [speciatim].

Asphal. Authores equidem tuos non legi, neque quid in hac re affirmant, multum requiro; non enim suffragiis et calculorum multitudine Philosophica bella confici crediderim. Sed exemplum tuum an accommodatum sit, et tale ut positam difficultatem elevet ipsus, arbiter esto. Ego enim duo in eo desidero; atque imprimis eandem esse formam prorsus inficior.

Asphal. Your Authors indeed I have not read, nor do I much inquire after [requiro] what they affirm in this matter; for I should not believe that Philosophical wars are finished [confici] by votes [suffragiis] and a multitude of pebbles [calculorum]. But whether your example is fitting [accommodatum], and such as to lift [elevet] the difficulty that has been posed, be yourself [ipsus] judge. For I find two [things] wanting [desidero] in it; and first of all I altogether deny [inficior] that the form is the same.

Vide, sodes, Ereunius plures stellas ipsa re a nobis infinite distare accipit et infert, haec itaque (quae una ex illis est) distat. Tu Equum id est unum ex multis tibi necessarium allegas, et negas inferri hunc esse necessarium: et merito quidem, sed non vides in antecedente disparem esse vocum rationem et aliam quidem universaliter, aliam particulariter accipi? Expone siquidem voces et cum dicitur plures stellae infinite absunt, non vides hoc dictum ex pluribus, nullam non infinite distare? vide nunc tuam. Equus est mihi necessarius, num tantumdem valet ac si dictum foret, nullus non est necessarius? an potius quod aliquis est mihi necessarius? Quid itaque mirum quod non i-[p. 15]dem ex utraque sequitur assumptione?

See, please [sodes]: Ereunius takes [it] that more [plures] stars are in very fact [ipsa re] infinitely distant from us, and infers: 'this one therefore (which is one of them) is distant'. You allege a Horse, that is, one out of many, [to be] necessary to you, and deny that it is inferred that this one is necessary: and rightly indeed; but do you not see that in the antecedent the reason [ratio] of the words is unequal [disparem], and [that it] is taken one way universally, another particularly? For [siquidem] expound the words; and when it is said 'more stars are infinitely away', do you not see this [to be] said of more [ex pluribus]: 'none [is] not infinitely distant'? See now yours. 'A horse is necessary to me': is it worth as much [tantumdem valet] as if it had been said, 'none is not necessary'? or rather that 'some one is necessary to me'? What wonder therefore that not the sa-[p. 15]me follows from each assumption?

Alterum quod in propositione tua accuso, est, quod materia propositionum immaniter sit diversa. Ereunii siquidem propositio de rebus actu in rerum natura existentibus agit, tua propositio rerum in potentia existentium conditionem habet. Non potes autem ignarus esse, rem quae actu sit Entis et unius, i. [id est] explicatam et definitam conditionem habere. in potentia vero existentium confusas et unitas esse rationes.

The other [thing] which I find fault with [accuso] in your proposition is that the matter [materia] of the propositions is monstrously [immaniter] different. For the proposition of Ereunius treats of things existing in act [actu] in the nature of things; your proposition has the condition of things existing in potency [in potentia]. But you cannot be ignorant that a thing which is in act has the condition of Being [Entis] and of One [unius], i.e. an unfolded [explicatam] and defined condition; but that the reasons [rationes] of things existing in potency are confused and united [unitas].

Sortes ubi natus est, certam figuram et speciem et personam habet, cum vero adhuc in patris semine esset, nondum magis Sortes quam Callias erat. Sic cum equo veheris, equus tuus certos habet limites, certas notas, et uno hoc equo uteris. Prius autem quam vecteris, dum adhuc uti potes, sed nondum uteris, ille quo uti potes neque longam cervicem habet neque brevem; neque spadix est neque gilvus sed horum quilibet. Cernis igitur quam iniquum sit ex una harum materia transcendere in aliam, vel expectare ut sequela, quam in una efficacem tenes, ad reliquam transferatur.

Sortes, when he has been born, has a certain figure and appearance [speciem] and person; but when he was still in [his] father's seed, he was not yet more Sortes than Callias. So when you are carried by a horse, your horse has certain limits, certain marks [notas], and you use this one horse. But before you are carried [vecteris], while you are still able to use [one], but are not yet using [one], that [horse] which you are able to use has neither a long neck nor a short; nor is it bay [spadix] nor dun [gilvus], but any of these. You perceive therefore how unfair it is to pass over [transcendere] from one of these matters into another, or to expect that a consequence [sequela] which you hold effective in one be transferred to the other.

Andab. Non eo inficias esse aliquam exempli disparitatem, neque satis demiror non perspectam accuratissimis Philosophis; et eam credo causam quod attenti ad summam rei, tales minutias leviori oculo lustrabant. Sed non multum interest: constat enim hanc esse [p. 16] infiniti naturam ut tantummodo partes infinite distantes habere possit indeterminate, non autem determinate:

Andab. I do not go to deny [Non eo inficias] that there is some disparity of the example, nor do I sufficiently wonder [neque satis demiror] [that it was] not perceived by the most accurate Philosophers; and I believe this [to be] the cause, that, attentive to the sum [summam] of the matter, they surveyed such minutiae with a lighter eye. But it does not matter much: for it is established [constat] that this is [p. 16] the nature of the infinite, that it can have parts infinitely distant only indeterminately [indeterminate], but not determinately [determinate]:

unde accusare infinitatem hoc nomine tantumdem est, ac si contra naturam hominis allegaretur quod rationalis sit: Naturae enim rerum quales sunt, accipiendae sunt, non novae effingendae; Clarissimum siquidem est si determinata aliqua pars ponatur ab alia, item determinata infinito spatio recessisse, quod infinita longitudo finibus duobus inclusa constituatur, quae est clarissima contradictio.

whence to accuse infinity [infinitatem] on this account [hoc nomine] is as much as if it were alleged against the nature of man that he is rational: for the natures of things are to be accepted such as they are, not to be fashioned [effingendae] new; for [siquidem] it is most clear, if some determinate part be posited to have receded from another, likewise determinate, by an infinite space, that an infinite length is constituted enclosed by two ends [finibus], which is a most clear contradiction.

Ereu. Quam places nunc et tu et haec tua dissertatio! sed enim quis alius superest modus naturam in medium propositam examinandi, talisne sit quae existentiam et locum in natura mereatur, an vero in tenebras et deserta impossibilibus habitata releganda sit, praeter hunc, ut utrum quae de natura asseruntur, inter sese consentiant, an vero oppositionem aliquam implicent, inquiratur? Aut ipse tu qua alia trutina chimaerae expendis valorem quam ut draconis et leonis per medium ignem connexionem improbes eamque propterea abdicas?

Ereu. How you please [me] now, both you and this dissertation of yours! But indeed what other mode remains of examining a nature put forward into the middle [in medium propositam], whether it be such as deserves existence and place in nature, or rather is to be banished into darkness and deserts inhabited by impossibles, besides this: that it be inquired whether the things which are asserted about the nature agree among themselves, or rather involve [implicent] some opposition? Or you yourself, with what other balance [trutina] do you weigh the value of a chimaera than that you disapprove [improbes] the connexion of a dragon and a lion through fire in the middle [per medium ignem], and therefore disown [abdicas] it?

Si igitur fateris finitum esse quod terminis clauditur et quaecumque determinate distant, spatium claudere, et quod consequens est, finite distare, evidens quoque sit si infinitum ponatur, quascumque eius partes determinate [p. 17] distare, confectum profecto est singulas, i. [id est] omnes eius partes finito a se invicem esse remotas intervallo, hoc est ipsum totum finitum esse. Quare frigida est haec excusatio, hanc esse infiniti naturam, cum tantumdem possit, ac si diceretur infiniti esse naturam, ut oppositionem et impossibilitatem involvat.

If therefore you confess that that is finite which is closed by terms [terminis], and that whatever [things] are determinately distant enclose a space, and, what is consequent, are finitely distant, let it also be evident [evidens sit], if the infinite be posited, that whatever parts of it [are] determinately [p. 17] distant—assuredly it is made out [confectum est] that each [singulas], i.e. all its parts, are removed from one another by a finite interval, that is, that the whole itself is finite. Wherefore cold [frigida] is this excuse, that this is the nature of the infinite, since it is worth as much [tantumdem possit] as if it were said that it is the nature of the infinite that it involves opposition and impossibility.

terms: infinitas can be 'infinitude' or 'boundlessness'; infinitum can be the noun 'the infinite' or the adjective.
The topic of the Knot: White's Aristotelian denial of an actually infinite magnitude (cf. Physics III.5), against the infinite universe of Bruno and others that Andabata defends.
the Roman double step (5 feet); also 'step'.
Used as the unit of measure in the thought-experiment; 'pedes', 'digiti', 'palmus' and 'milliaria' (feet, fingers, palm, miles) are the other units, all rendered literally.
Scholastic: a 'signable' (signabilis) part is one that can be marked off as this part. The dispute turns on whether infinitely distant parts can be designated singly.
'definitely / indefinitely'; 'as this one / as some one or other'.
Andabata's defence: in the infinite, parts are infinitely distant only 'indeterminately' (taken in common), never as a determinate this-one.
in communi / universaliter / universim / particulariter / singulariter / singulatim / speciatim
in common / universally / universally [universim] / particularly / singly / singly [singulatim] / specifically
Logical vocabulary of quantified propositions and their 'descent' to singulars.

Asphalius' reply uses the scholastic theory of supposition: a universal (distributive) term allows descent to each singular, a particular one does not. Hence 'plures stellae' read as 'none is not distant' (distributive), and 'equus' as 'some horse' (particular).
Technical term of supposition theory (descensus copulative/disjunctive).
Logical term: the proposition from which the consequent is inferred.
Scholastic term for a valid inference or its rule.
In rhetoric (Hermagoras, Cicero, Quintilian) a thesis is a general question without persons or circumstances, a hypothesis a particular case.
Asphalius asks Andabata to bring his general claim (many paces are infinitely distant) down to a particular case (this pace). The words do not mean 'claim' and 'assumption' in the modern sense.
Aristotelian. Asphalius: things in act have a defined, 'unfolded' (explicata) condition; things in potency have 'confused and united' reasons (rationes).
Transcendentals of scholastic metaphysics: whatever actually exists is a being and is one, i.e. determinate. Capitalised as printed (Entis).
Aristotelian 'poson': the quantified thing, as distinct from quantitas (quantity).
Scholastic: a predicate 'competit' to a subject when it truly belongs to it.
Kept as 'reason' for consistency with the glossary; the context here is the nature (ratio) of quantity and the sense (ratio) of words.
A borrowing from Virgil, Aeneid 1.257–8, Jupiter to Venus: 'Parce metu, Cytherea: manent immota tuorum / fata tibi'. Andabata plays Jupiter calming Ereunius.
Satin tibi praesens es? / satin sanus es?
Are you sufficiently present to yourself? / are you sufficiently sane?
'Are you in your right mind?' / 'Are you quite well?'
Comic idiom of Plautus and Terence ('satin sanus es?'); the two speakers volley it back and forth.
'with your very latest breath', i.e. just now.
Means 'in the speech you have just made', not 'on your deathbed'.
Proverbial; cf. Terence, Phormio 780 'in eodem luto haesitas'.
by votes and a multitude of pebbles
calculi are the pebbles used for voting (and counting).
Asphalius rejects deciding philosophy by counting authorities. This is a commonplace of the new philosophy.

'Sortes' is the scholastic logicians' stock form of 'Socrates', and Callias is Aristotle's stock example of an individual. Asphalius means that in the seed (in potency) the individual is not yet determined.
spadix: chestnut-brown, date-coloured; gilvus: pale yellow, dun or cream.
Horse colours from Virgil, Georgics 3.82 ('honesti spadices glaucique, color deterrimus albis et gilvo').
In logic, the 'matter' of a proposition (necessary, contingent, impossible) or its content, as against its form.
Asphalius' two objections are the form (universal vs particular) and the matter (act vs potency) of the propositions.
chimaera … draconis et leonis per medium ignem connexio
a chimaera … the connexion of a dragon and a lion through fire in the middle
The Homeric Chimaera (Iliad 6.181: lion in front, serpent behind, she-goat in the middle, breathing fire). In scholastic logic it is the standard example of an impossible being (ens rationis).
a pair of scales; 'standard of judgement'.
Rhetorical term for a lame argument or excuse.
I do not go to deny
stand off / be away / be distant / stand apart / recede
Kept distinct so that the reader can see White's variation.
notes: Unit: Dialogue I, Knot ii, part 1 of 2. PDF pp. 20–28 = printed pp. 9–17. It starts at Ereunius' 'Quoniam utrique sedit eadem voluntas' on p. 9, where the margin has 'Nodus II. Mundum non esse infinitum' (printed with tildes: 'Mundū … infinitū'). It ends at the close of Ereunius' speech '…impossibilitatem involvat' near the top of p. 17. Part 2 starts on the same page (PDF 28) with Andabata's 'Non tam facile quam credis confectum est negotium', where the margin has 'Argumenta pro infinito solvuntur' (Arguments for the infinite are resolved). The offset of +11 holds throughout (p. 17 = PDF 28).

Rows: one row per speech. Long speeches by Asphalius and Andabata are split at sentence breaks so that Latin and English line up. Printed page breaks are marked [p. n] in both columns, with the split word shown as 'quic-[p. 10]quam'.

Conventions (as in glossary.md): long s → s; æ/œ → ae/oe; tildes expanded (Mundū → Mundum, nā → nam); consonantal u → v; accents dropped (à, cùm, verò, imò). 'Ereunij' → Ereunii. 'i.' (= id est) is kept and expanded as 'i. [id est]'. Spellings as printed: 'coelum/coeli', 'caelestis' (p. 9) beside 'coelestium' (p. 10), 'Authores', 'pronunciasti', 'inficias', 'ipsus' (archaic for ipse), 'expectare'.

Printed oddities kept: 'abdicas' (p. 16) is indicative where the parallel 'improbes' is subjunctive; it is kept and translated as printed. Asphalius' question mark after 'agnoscas?' (p. 12) is kept, though the sentence goes on with 'sed ut …'. 'Mathematico tecum more vel sermone' is taken as 'in the Mathematical manner or speech' (more and sermone both ablative with Mathematico).

Sense notes: (a) p. 11, 'contiguus ergo passus iam numeratis abest passibus' is read as: the pace next to the supposed infinitely distant one is distant from us only by 'numbered' (finite) paces, so adding one pace would make the finite infinite. (b) p. 13, 'Cras eundum mihi est quo hodie debueram' is read with 'ire' understood: 'whither I ought to have [gone] today' (Andabata was on his way when the storm stopped him, Knot i). (c) pp. 16–17, Ereunius' last sentence is an anacoluthon: 'evidens quoque sit … quascumque eius partes determinate distare' breaks off, and a new main clause 'confectum profecto est …' takes over. The English keeps the break with a dash.

Uncertain: 'absistere' (p. 10) is used in an unusual sense ('be distant'); the reading is clear on the page. 'vecteris' (p. 15) is taken as the present subjunctive passive of vecto ('before you are carried'). No illegible words.

Verification pass: the transcription was compared again with the page images, and the English with the Latin, sentence by sentence (cases, tenses, moods, negatives, comparatives, omissions). This gave 5 corrections: (1) p. 9 'caelestis' had been normalised to 'coelestis'; restored to the printed spelling. (2) p. 12 'ipsus … arbiter esto': 'ipsus' had been attached to 'elevet' (the example itself); it is masculine and goes with the imperative ('be yourself judge'). (3) p. 13 'debueram' had been rendered 'I ought'; corrected to 'I ought [to have gone]'. (4) pp. 16–17 'evidens quoque sit' had been rendered as indicative ('it is also evident'); corrected to the subjunctive 'let it also be evident'. (5) p. 14 'quod non idem … sequitur' had 'the same [conclusion]'; the supplied word was dropped as an addition not needed by the Latin.
